about: Sarre (Serræ), the king's toll landing in the middle of the Wantsum, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/sarre.md and the spine (cast.wighelm, cast.thorkell, cast.aethelheard, cast.gervold; threads black_stones, silver_road, price_of_england). A draft for the user to overwrite. Read the note first. Woven with the other ports of the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways with Fordwic, Dofras and Lundenwic, beats added there and at Gipeswic, a small story of the ale-wife's lost ship that ends on the breaking beach at Lundenwic (sarre.sheldrake), and the region's cards (Data/encounters/england_south_east_793.json) hung on the sites and the beats.
note: Sarre in these years is known from one charter of 763 or 764 (Sawyer 29) and from what sailed past it. Nothing of 793 to 1066 has been dug here, and no person of Sarre is named in any text. So every site but the grave field is ours, every person but Abbess Cwenthryth and Ealdorman Ealhhere is ours, and each says so in its source. We do not know that the toll of 763 was still taken in 793, or that it had stopped: the game takes it. There is no church, no mint, no wall and no bridge here in the game's years, and the ferry is likely but not recorded before about 1414.

ports.summary: Serræ is a landing under a chalk bank on the Thanet shore of the Wantsum, where the strait is narrowest and the two tides meet. The king's toll men take toll on ships here, the road from Canterbury crosses the water, and every hull that goes inside Thanet between the Channel and the Thames lies here a tide. A merchant comes for the man who knows the fords, for the abbess's ships and her freedom from toll, for Thanet corn, salt and oysters, and for news that is half a day younger than anywhere else in Kent.
ports.seasons: Ships pass from about Easter to Martinmas, and lie here to change one tide for the other. Thanet's corn is cut from Lammas; Saint Mildrith's day falls in high summer, thirteen days into July, and the island walks to Minster for it; oysters are gathered in the cold months and salt is boiled in the dry ones. In winter the saltings flood and the road to the crossing is a line of stakes in grey water.

history.text: Augustine lands on Thanet with about forty companions. The island is reckoned at six hundred hides, and the Wantsum that parts it from Kent is about three furlongs over and can be crossed in two places only.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.25 (written about 731; L.C. Jane's translation, 1903); dossier 1

history.text: The dead of Sarre are laid on the down above the landing with swords, amber, scales and gaming pieces, until about this time. More than 270 graves have been found; there were more swords here, one to every ten graves, than in any grave field its digger knew.
history.source: J. Brent, Archaeologia Cantiana 5-7 (1863-68); dossier 2. The year is the end of a span (6th to mid 7th century), not a record

history.text: King Wihtred's law fines gifts to idols and meat eaten in a fast. A stranger who leaves the track and neither shouts nor blows his horn may be killed or taken as a thief.

King Æthelbald of Mercia lets Abbess Eadburh of Minster off half the toll on a ship at London. She had bought the ship from a man named Leubucus, and had built the church of Peter and Paul for Saint Mildrith's body.

King Eadberht of Kent gives Abbess Sigeburh of Minster the toll on the carriage of two ships that was his by right 'in the place called ad Serrae', and all tribute and toll on a third, lately built in the minster, at the public places Fordwic and Seorre. If that ship is broken, worn out with age or wrecked, another may take her place; and what the nuns gain by her trading they must offer to the king at Fordwic. It is the only time Sarre is named before the Conquest.
history.source: Sawyer 29 (763 or 764): esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/29.html, the dossier's rendering

history.text: Offa of Mercia rules Kent himself; Kent has no king of its own until he dies.
history.source: dossier 3 (list of the kings of Kent)

history.text: Offa dies on 29 July. Eadberht Præn takes Kent, and Archbishop Æthelheard flees Canterbury.
This year Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, laid waste Kent as far as the Marsh, took Eadberht Præn and led him bound into Mercia. Cuthred, the king's brother, is set over Kent.

Cwenthryth, King Coenwulf's daughter, is named as abbess: she holds Minster in Thanet and Reculver with Winchcombe. Archbishop Wulfred claims both Kentish houses, and the quarrel runs past her father's death.
Kent passes from Mercia to Ecgberht of Wessex. King Baldred is driven north over the Thames.
By about this year Cwenthryth has given up Minster and Reculver to Archbishop Wulfred.
King Æthelstan and Ealdorman Ealhhere fight in ships at Sandwich and take nine of the enemy's. This year the heathen men for the first time stay the winter on Thanet.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851 (Ingram 1823); chronicle_793.json 851-thanet-canterbury-london. Some copies say Sheppey

history.text: Ealhhere with the men of Kent and Huda with the men of Surrey fight the heathen army on Thanet. Many are slain and drowned on either hand, and both ealdormen are killed.
The heathen army sits on Thanet and makes peace with the men of Kent for a promise of money. Under cover of the peace it steals inland by night and overruns all east Kent.
King Eadred gives Reculver, with its land in Thanet, to Christ Church at Canterbury. Some doubt the charter.
This year King Edgar ordered all Thanet-land to be plundered. A later writer gives the reason: the islanders had robbed merchants come from York.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 969 (Ingram 1823); Roger of Wendover, who says 974, known to the dossier only at second hand (?)

history.text: Thanet is overrun by a ship-army, the same year that Hamwic is sacked.
Soon after Lammas Thorkell's army comes to Sandwich. East Kent buys peace for three thousand pounds.
Canterbury falls between the Nativity of Saint Mary and Michaelmas. Abbess Leofrun is among those taken; she is counted the last abbess of Minster.
Saint Mildrith's body is carried from Minster to Saint Augustine's at Canterbury, by King Cnut's gift, against fierce opposition on the island. Her lands go with her.

Lothen and Yrling come to Sandwich with twenty-five ships and take men, gold and silver beyond counting. Then they go about Thanet, but the land's folk withstand them and deny them both landing and water.
Earl Godwine and Harold go with their ships from Sandwich to the North-mouth and so toward London: through the Wantsum and past Sarre, as it is read.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1052; Brent 1863 and Perkins 2007 for the reading (Ingram prints 'the Nore'); dossier 5 and 8

eras.text: Offa's last years. The toll men are a Mercian king's, the pennies are his new heavy ones, and Frankish hulls are turned away from English shores. The abbess's three ships pass free and everyone else counts them. The wic-reeve of Lundenwic comes down the strait now and then on the king's business.

Eadberht Præn's rising. Nobody at the toll place is sure whose toll it is; the archbishop has fled; in 798 the Mercian army burns its way across Kent. Ships go through without stopping, and the ale-house bars its door at dusk.

Mercian Kent, quiet for a merchant. King and archbishop quarrel over who owns the minsters of Thanet and Reculver, and from about 811 the abbess is the king's own daughter. Letters go up and down the strait and it is wise to carry none.

West Saxon Kent. The toll man answers to a new king's reeve; the minsters are the archbishop's. Sheppey is harried in 835 and a watch is kept on the down. More ships use the south mouth, where a landing at Sandwich is growing.

The heathen men winter on Thanet. Some summers the strait is theirs and the landing is empty; the ealdorman's levy fights on the island in 853 and both ealdormen die. The toll man asks whom you mean to sell to.

A long quiet. The great army goes north; burhs are built elsewhere; one king takes the toll from Chester round to Gipeswic. Reculver and its Thanet land go to Christ Church. In 969 King Edgar has the whole island plundered for robbing merchants, and for a while after a stranger's goods are very safe here.

The ship-armies come back. Thanet is overrun in 980, the fleets lie at Sandwich in 991, 1006, 1009 and 1013, and the island pays its part of three thousand pounds. The saltings silt a little more each year and the big ships no longer come through loaded.

Cnut's peace and after. Sandwich is the port of the strait and Sarre is its back door: a ferry, a few boats, salt and corn. Saint Mildrith is carried off to Canterbury in 1030. In 1048 the islanders keep twenty-five ships from landing or watering, and in 1052 Godwine's fleet goes through to London.

sites.name: The lying-ground under the chalk
sites.see: A low white bank of chalk facing west and south, and under it a shelf of shingle and grey mud where a dozen hulls lie on their bilges with their masts down. Beyond them the strait: brown water a few bowshots wide, saltings on the far side, the Kent shore a low green line. At the meeting of the tides the water stands still and the boats all swing at once. Tar, weed, wet chalk, a mallet on a trenail.
sites.source: boats lay 'under the chalk cliffs facing the west and south' (Brent 1863); 'a place where the shipping often lay at anchor' (Hasted 1800); the tides flow in at both mouths and meet at Sarre (Hasted). The wright and his slip are ours

sites.name: The king's toll place
sites.see: Where the track comes down through the bank, a hurdle fence, a bench, and a post with notches cut in it for every ship of the season. A grey-haired man sits with a bundle of tally sticks and a small balance in a wooden case; a boy holds a horse. Whoever lands walks past him, and he has already counted their strakes. On some days a second man stands behind him in a green cloak, saying little.
sites.source: the king's toll-collectors (thelonearii) at 'the place called ad Serrae', a public place (Sawyer 29). No building is known; the fence, bench and post are ours. The man in the green cloak is the spine's cast.wighelm, who is met here

sites.name: The crossing
sites.see: A line of stakes runs out across the mud to the low-water channel, and at the end of it a broad flat boat with two oars lies waiting. On the far side the Canterbury road comes down between saltings. At the ebb the ferryman wades out with a passenger on his shoulders and tips him in over the gunwale; at the flood the boat comes to the bank and nobody is carried. Curlews, and a horn blown from the Kent shore.
sites.source: the road from Canterbury crosses into Thanet here (dossier 1). A boat crossing in 793 is likely, not recorded (?): the ferry is first drawn about 1414, a boatman carrying a passenger on his shoulders to the boat (Perkins 2007; Brent 1863). Bede's two fording places (I.25)

sites.name: The strand market
sites.see: On the dry shingle above the weed line, sacks of corn stood open, a heap of grey salt on a hide, cheeses, fleeces tied in bundles, baskets of oysters under wet weed. A ship's people sell off the gunwale: a cask, a pair of dark quernstones, a crate of spouted pots in straw. Two men stand by every bargain and do nothing but watch it. Brine, sheep, a broached cask.
sites.source: invented: no cargo, price or market day is recorded at Sarre (dossier 8). The goods are the region's and the island's: corn (Bede's fruitful Thanet), salt and fish (Domesday for Minster and Monkton), wool, cloth and hides out, wine, querns, pots and glass in (dossier 4). The two watchers are the witnesses a Kentish buyer needs (Law of Hlothhere and Eadric 16)

sites.name: Tidburh's ale-house
sites.see: A long thatched house end-on to the wind, halfway up the bank, with a pole and a bunch of green leaves over the door. Inside, a hearth on the floor, benches, a tub of ale, a board marked in squares with little bone counters on it, yellow with handling. A heap of oyster shells by the door is higher than a child. Skippers waiting for the other tide sit here and say what things cost in Lundenwic three days ago.
sites.source: invented. The counters and dice are the kind found in the graves on the down (about fifty bone gaming counters in grave 6, forty more and two dice in grave 198: Brent 1866, 1868). The oyster riddle is given here (riddles_793.json; unlocks_793.json text.exeter_77_oyster)

sites.name: The abbess's ship-house
sites.see: A long shed of split oak at the north end of the strand, its doors wide enough for a hull, a wooden cross nailed over them. Inside, a ship's gear laid out by kind: oars in a rack, a rolled sail, a stack of sealed jars, corn in bins. A nun in an undyed gown stands at a slanted board with a wax tablet. A small ship lies on rollers before the doors, old and much mended, with a newer one afloat beyond her.
sites.source: the minster's three toll-free ships, one bought from Leubucus and one 'lately built in the minster' (Sawyer 91, 29). That they kept a shed at Sarre is ours; Minster itself lies an hour's walk east. After 1030 the house's lands are Saint Augustine's (dossier 5)

sites.name: The cross above the landing
sites.see: On the lip of the bank, where the track tops the chalk, a wooden cross taller than a man with a flat stone at its foot. From here both ends of the strait can be seen: north, far off, the grey Roman wall at Reculver with the minster's roof inside it; south, the broken walls of Richborough. A priest walks over from Reculver on feast days and says Mass in the open; on other days there is a bowl for alms and somebody's candle stub.
sites.source: invented. Sarre has no church in the game's years (Saint Giles is 11th century at the earliest (?) and is not in Domesday). Western Thanet looked to Saint Mary's minster at Reculver, about an hour and a half on foot (the dossier's inference). Reculver's later twin towers are not to be drawn

sites.name: The old graves on the down
sites.see: Above the landing the chalk rises to a bare green shoulder, cropped by sheep, with shallow dips in the turf in rows. Nothing stands on it. From the top the whole country lies open for miles: the strait from mouth to mouth, the island's cornfields, sails off the North Foreland. Larks, wind, and now and then something green and metal in a molehill.
sites.source: the grave field on Sarre Down, 'commanding the country for miles around' (Brent 1863): 6th and 7th centuries, already old in 793. No mounds are recorded, and none are drawn. That its people were still remembered is ours

sites.name: The ploughland under the down
sites.see: Long strips of brown and green running up from the marsh edge to the foot of the down. Eight oxen in pairs drag a heavy plough; a man leans on the tail and a boy walks backwards before the leaders with a goad, singing to them. Gulls follow the furrow. At the marsh end a lord's man sometimes stands with a hawk on his fist, looking at the herons.
sites.source: Thanet's 'fruitful fields' (dossier 3); the eight-ox plough is the English one of the laws and of Domesday (?). The plough riddle is given here by a ploughman of Thanet (riddles_793.json; unlocks_793.json text.exeter_21_plough). Hawking on the marsh: story/town_games_793.json names Sarre

sites.name: The saltings
sites.see: South of the landing the shore breaks into creeks and grey-green marsh. At low water women with baskets walk the mud bent double, and a row of stakes with wattle between them shows where a fish weir stands. Further off a thread of brown smoke rises from a salt pan. Everything shines; the smell is weed, mud and smoke.
sites.source: a salt-pit and two fisheries at Minster, a fishery and a salt work at Monkton, in 1086 (Hasted, from Domesday); Roman pits at Sarre full of oyster shells (Brent 1863). That salt and oysters were worked off Sarre itself in 793 is our guess (?)

people.name: Dunwalh
people.trait: The king's toll man at Sarre, as his father was: has counted the same three free ships past his post for thirty years and can tell a hull by the sound of her oars.
people.want: A quiet season, a king who stays king, and one honest witness he does not have to fetch from the ale-house.
people.fear: Being the man who took toll for the wrong king; in Offa's day, Offa.
people.voice: Slow Kentish, exact about numbers, vague about kings. Says 'the king' and lets you decide which.
people.looks: Nearing fifty, lean, grey hair cut at the jaw, a brown cloak pinned with a small round brooch, tally sticks in his belt and a little bronze balance in a wooden case.
knows: what toll a ship of your size owes here, and which ships owe none
the law on buying before witnesses, and who will stand witness for a cup
who rules Kent this month, as far as anybody at Sarre has been told
which hulls went through on the last two tides, and which way
when the wic-reeve of Lundenwic is next looked for

ties.note: his wife is the wic-reeve's sister; the reeve comes down the strait, checks his tallies, and hears what is coming up the river two tides early
her ships pass free and he is certain there are more of them every year
they were boys on this strand together; the ferryman tells him who crossed
an ale score nobody has reckoned since Offa took Kent
the archbishop is Offa's man too; when he fled in 796 Dunwalh did not ask which way
passed Leofstan's ship through to the Channel before the ports were shut, and has wondered since
Tilred at the Stour landing takes the same king's toll; they send each other the count of the abbess's ships, and it never agrees
lets certain things the plough turns up go unreported, and reminds the ploughman of it at Lammas
in his last year the abbess is the king's own daughter, and expects the king's toll man to remember it
not he but his post: a generation on, the notches he began are read by the ealdorman of Kent himself, who asks who cut them

lines.greet: A Frisian, by the stem. You lie here, you pay here. By the ship, not by what is in her. I look inside only if you make me.
lines.greet_again: I have you on the post already. Third notch from the top, the small one. Sit down. Who is king where you came from?
rumour: The Franks' king has shut his shores to our keels, so ours are shut to his. You are his man or you are not. Think before the reeve asks.
The abbess has three ships free by the old king's word. I count four crosses on four stems each summer. I am told my counting is at fault.
They say the priest who calls himself king had his hair cut for God once. Kent has had stranger. I take the toll and keep the tallies.
lines.saying: A man who weighs silver for strangers needs his spear as much as his scale.
lines.trusted: Come at the slack and I will pass you with the minster's ships. Do not thank me where the nun can hear.
lines.farewell: Go out with the ebb by the south mouth. If you meet the reeve, I asked you everything.

people.source: invented. The office is the king's toll-collector of Sawyer 29; no toll man or reeve of Sarre is named anywhere. His saying turns the 1866 editor's remark on the man buried with scales and a spear (Brent 1866). The witness rule is Hlothhere and Eadric 16

people.name: Dudda
people.trait: The ferryman of the crossing: strong as an ox, knows both fords and every bank of the strait by the feel of the mud, and talks without stopping from one shore to the other.
people.want: His son to keep the ferry and not go to sea in a Frisian's boat; a new hull before the old one opens under a bishop.
people.fear: A passenger drowned off his shoulders; a bridge.
people.voice: Loud, cheerful, wet to the thigh. Starts in the middle of a story and assumes you know the people.
people.looks: Early thirties in 793, broad and short, bare legs grey with mud, a tunic kilted up into his belt, a cow's horn on a cord and a long ash pole.
knows: the two places the strait can be forded, and at what state of tide
the channel through to the North-mouth by Reculver and to the south mouth by Stonar bank
where the two tides meet today and how long the slack will last
everyone who has crossed to Canterbury this week and what they were carrying
which of the island's men will stand witness and which will say anything

ties.note: tells the toll man who crossed, and is told who is expected
his elder sister; she still gives him orders
they have disputed one strip of marsh pasture since their fathers did
sends the pilgrims he carries over to the monk's guest hall, and has never seen it
Wulfric of Dofras says the inside passage is for men afraid of the Foreland; Dudda says it is for men who mean to arrive
carried the archbishop's people over in 796 at night and was paid in a blessing
the hayward at Fordwic sells him a foal now and then and walks the whole road to the crossing without a word, which Dudda fills

lines.greet: You want over, or you want through? Over is a penny for six men and I carry you the wet part. Through is another matter.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the small boat. You touched on the north bank coming in, I heard her. Next time ask me first.
rumour: Three for Rome went over at Whitsun with staffs and one bundle between them. The bundle was heavier than their sins, I can tell you. I carried it.
The archbishop's men crossed in the dark with a chest and no torches. I asked nothing. I am asking you nothing now.
There are sails off the Foreland that do not come in. The shepherd on the down counted them twice. Honest ships come in.
lines.saying: The flood comes in at both doors and meets itself here. Like my wife and her mother.
lines.earth: No snakes on Thanet. The earth kills them. A learned man wrote it. I will fill you a bag for a farthing's worth of ale.
lines.farewell: Keep the stakes on your left hand till the church at Reculver opens behind the point. Then you are in the sea and not my trouble.

people.source: invented; a ferryman at Sarre is recorded only from about 1414, carrying a passenger on his shoulders (Perkins 2007). The horn law is Wihtred 28. Thanet's earth killing snakes is Isidore of Seville, about 620, through the dossier (7). The night crossing is ours, from Æthelheard's flight in 796

people.name: Tidburh
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house and an oyster bed of her own: a shipman's widow who hears every price twice, once going up the strait and once coming down, and remembers both.
people.want: To know what happened to her husband's ship, which went out by the North-mouth nine summers ago for Lundenwic; and her cousin over the water sent word that she is alive.
people.fear: An empty strand; soldiers of any king in her house.
people.voice: Dry and quick. Answers a question with the price of something, and is usually answering it.
people.looks: Near forty, tall and spare, a linen head-cloth, a grey gown with two small disc brooches, sleeves pushed up, an oyster knife on her girdle and red hands.
knows: what corn, salt, wool and wine fetched at Lundenwic and at Fordwic by the last ship from each
which skippers are waiting on which tide, and who needs a hand at the oars
the riddles the island tells, and who invented none of them
who on Thanet is buying and who only looks
where her brother the ferryman is, when he is not where he should be

ties.note: her younger brother; she lent him the price of the ferry
her cousin, a Kentish woman who married a Frankish wine man and keeps a guest house over the water; no word since the ports were shut
sells the nun oysters for fast days and tells her what the skippers say about the minster's ships
he drinks on a tally she never reckons, and in return she is never short of a witness
the wic-reeve's men drink here and pay in promises
Beornflæd at Dofras says her ale is older and so better; Tidburh says old is the word for it
her mother's sister's daughter on the marsh edge at Fordwic: cheeses and gossip go between them with the carters
the yellow counters on her board came out of his furrow, and neither of them tells the priest

lines.greet: Sit by the door, your boots are the strand's. Ale is the island's barley. Wine is for the abbess and for God, in that order.
lines.greet_again: You came back, so Lundenwic did not eat you. What was wheat there? Tell me true and the first cup is mine to give.
rumour: Salt is up. The pans at Minster lost a week to rain, and every boat wants it before the herring. Buy today or do not complain to me.
The nuns want wine for the altar and none comes over. A cask landed quietly would be paid for twice. I did not say it.
lines.saying: News is like oysters. Fresh off the boat, or leave it.
lines.husband: He went out by the North-mouth at Lammas tide with corn for the Strand. If you hear of a ship called the Sheldrake, tell me. Whatever it is.
lines.cousin: If you lie at the Franks' wic on the Canche, ask for Wulfgifu's house. Say Tidburh still has the blue cup and has not broken it.
lines.farewell: God keep you off the banks. And pay my brother before he carries you, not after.

people.source: invented. Her cousin is quentovic.wulfgifu (places/quentovic.json). The minster's ships worked Thanet, the Wantsum and the Thames (Sawyer 86, 91, 29); the lost ship and its name are ours

people.name: Cwenburh
people.trait: A nun of Minster who keeps the reckoning of the house's ships: knows the old king's charter by heart, the Latin and the sense, and has never yet lost an argument at the toll post.
people.want: Wine for the altar while the Frankish ports are shut; a sound hull in place of the oldest ship before she drowns somebody; a master for her who does not lie about freights.
people.fear: The clause that sends a new ship's gains to the king at Fordwic; a king who does not know the charter, or knows it too well.
people.voice: Calm and exact, a little amused. Quotes the charter as other people quote weather.
people.looks: About forty-five, small, straight-backed, an undyed wool gown and a dark veil, ink on her right thumb, a wax tablet on a cord and a ring of three keys.
knows: what the charter of King Eadberht frees and what it does not, clause by clause
what the minster needs this season: wine, wax, glass, oil, a book cover mended
what the minster sells: corn, salt, wool, cheese, and at what price before the strand hears it
which abbess rules at Minster this year and how she takes to merchants
the feast days, and so when the island will buy and when it will not

ties.note: he counts her ships; she counts his mistakes
hears from her what the skippers will not tell a nun
from 811 her abbess, a king's daughter who wants every tally explained twice
the archbishop is her house's father in God, and sends for its ship when he wants one
the abbot's clerk at Quentovic once passed the minster's wine in a shut year; she has not been able to repay it
the reeve at Fordwic, to whom the charter says her new ship's gains must be shown: she shows him what the charter requires, beautifully, and not a sack more
Eadhun at Christ Church copies the house's charters, so that one lies where the damp cannot reach it
her tenant under the down: he carts the minster's corn to the ship-house and tells her the harvest before the reeve hears it
the wic-reeve passes the minster's ship at the Strand as his grandfather's king ordered; she sends him the charter's words each spring in case he has forgotten them

lines.greet: You are the Frisian. The toll man said small and honest, which from him is praise. Do you carry wine? No? Then sit and hear what we need.
lines.greet_again: God's welcome. The last freight tallied to the penny. I mention it because it is rarer than you would think.
rumour: The charter says a ship broken, worn out with great age, or lost by wreck, which God forbid, may be replaced. Ours is two of those already.
The abbess keeps Saint Mildrith's day thirteen nights into July. The whole island comes. Bring wax before it and name your price, within reason.
The king and the archbishop both say Minster is theirs. We pray for both. We send the corn to whichever asks first with a seal.
lines.saying: The king's word is good. Written, sealed, and read aloud to his toll man, it is better.
lines.wine: No wine, no Mass. A Frankish cask cannot land at Lundenwic this year. It can land here, under our cross, if it is ours when it lands.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and bring back the jars. Empty ones too. They are counted.

people.source: invented; the abbess of 793 is not known (dossier 3). The clauses she quotes are Sawyer 29 in the dossier's rendering; the freedom at London is Sawyer 86, 91 and 143. Saint Mildrith's day is 13 July

people.name: Bynna
people.trait: A ploughman of Thanet who works the strips under the down, turns up dead men's things every spring, and has a riddle for most of them.
people.want: To know what a thing is worth before the priest says it must go back in the ground or the toll man says it is the king's.
people.fear: The people on the down, a little; the priest's opinion of what he keeps on his sill, more.
people.voice: Unhurried, sly, speaks in riddles and waits to see if you are quick. Says 'they' of the dead as of neighbours.
people.looks: Late twenties in 793, long and bony, sun-dark, a patched tunic and leg wrappings white with chalk, an ox goad over his shoulder and a stone like a small loaf in his pouch.
knows: what corn the island has to sell this year and who is holding it back
what comes out of the down under the plough: beads, bone counters, green metal, a little scale
the riddle of his own tool, and others he will trade for one he has not heard
the weather for the next two days, from the down
how many sails stand off the Foreland, since he can see them and the toll man cannot

ties.note: one strip of marsh pasture, two fathers, no end to it
the toll man has let certain finds go unreported, and reminds him
holds his strips of the minster and carts its corn to the ship-house
the yellow counters on her board came out of his furrow, and they do not tell the priest
old Lulla on the height at Dofras counts the same sails from the other side of the Foreland; a boy runs between them with the number (?)

lines.greet: A man from over the water. Good. Tell me this. I go nose down and am driven by my enemy, and what I tear, he sows. What am I?
lines.greet_again: The plough, yes, you had it last time. I have a harder one now. Sit on the headland. The oxen want a rest and so do I.
rumour: The barley is thin on the chalk and fat by the marsh. The abbess will sell after Lammas. Buy from the cart, before it reaches the strand.
I turned up a little pan of green bronze on a chain and small weights with it. Old emperors' heads, rubbed flat. Who weighs with an emperor?
Nine sails off the Foreland at first light, going north. Not ours. Ours do not sail nine together.
lines.saying: They lie facing east with their swords, waiting for a king who is not coming. We plough round them.
lines.stone: A thunder stone. It fell in a storm, my grandmother said. It has a star on it, look. I keep it where the priest does not sit.
lines.farewell: Blow your horn if you cut across my strips. I will know it is you by how badly.

people.source: invented. He is the 'ploughman of Thanet' who gives Exeter riddle 21 (riddles_793.json); his riddle is ours, on that riddle's lines, not a quotation. The finds are the kinds Brent dug from graves nobody had ploughed: a bronze balance with weights made of Roman coins ground down (grave 26), gaming counters, a fossil sea-urchin (grave 4). The 'thunder stone' name for the urchin is later English folk speech (?)

people.name: Cwenthryth
people.trait: King Coenwulf's daughter, abbess of Winchcombe, Reculver and Minster in Thanet at once: a ruler's child who holds her houses as her father's heir and yields nothing until she must.
people.want: To keep Minster and Reculver, their lands and their toll-free ships, against Archbishop Wulfred.
people.fear: Her father's death, which leaves her with the quarrel and without the king.
people.voice: Brief and courteous, a Mercian among Kentish people. Speaks to a merchant through the nun at her elbow and listens to the answer herself.
people.looks: A woman of perhaps thirty in 811, tall, pale, a fine dark veil and a gown of good blue cloth, a gold ring with a seal, a staff, two women and an armed thegn behind her.
knows: what her father the king intends in Kent, as far as she chooses to say
which of her ships is where, and what each has earned
what the archbishop claims and what he was offered
who at Lundenwic and at Canterbury can be trusted with a letter

ties.note: learned the house's charters from the old nun in her first year, and then asked for them in writing
expects the king's toll man to remember whose daughter she is
her father's old wic-reeve, who passed the minster's ships at the Strand without a word until he laid down his rod; the man after him has been told to do the same (?)
it is his successor Wulfred who claims her houses; she speaks of Canterbury as one neighbour

lines.greet: You master one of my ships, I am told, or wish to. Say which, and say what she earned last year. I have been told one figure already.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Good. My father the king asks what Frankish wine costs at the Strand. So do I, and I asked first.
rumour: The archbishop says these minsters are his. He has said so at Rome. Rome is far, and the ships are here.
Carry no letter out of Kent this season unless it has my seal or the king's. Others are being read on the road.
After Saint Mildrith's day I go to Winchcombe. What you want sealed, bring before it.
lines.saying: A charter is a memory that cannot be argued with. So keep the charter.
lines.later: The council has spoken and I have agreed. Your freedom stands, under the archbishop now. Be as honest with him as you were with me.
lines.farewell: Go safely. The nun will give you the tally. Bring it back as it is.

people.source: historical: Cwenthryth, daughter of Coenwulf of Mercia, named 811 to about 827, abbess of Winchcombe, Reculver and Minster in Thanet; she gave up the Kentish houses to Archbishop Wulfred by about 827 (dossier 3 and 5). Her birth and death are not recorded, and her looks and words are ours. A later legend, not of her own time, makes her the murderer of her brother Kenelm; the game does not use it

people.name: Ealhhere
people.trait: Ealdorman of Kent under the West Saxon kings: the man who fought the heathen in ships at Sandwich and took nine of theirs, and who means to do it again on land.
people.want: Ships, steersmen and warning: to know where the fleet lies before it knows where he is.
people.fear: A winter with the heathen men still on Thanet, and the levy gone home to its harvest.
people.voice: Blunt and good-humoured, a soldier's short questions. Asks a merchant what he saw, not what he thinks.
people.looks: A big man in his forties, sandy beard going grey, a mail shirt under a red cloak, a gold-hilted sword, a gilded cup at his saddle, and thirty riders who look like him.
knows: where the heathen fleet lay at the last report, and how old that report is
which landings in Kent are watched and which are not
what the king will pay for a ship's service for a summer
who has been selling corn to the camp on the island

ties.note: the Danes who hold Dorestad send ships this way; he would like to know which are theirs
not the old toll man but his post: the ealdorman reads the notches himself and asks who cut them
the host on the Strand sends him word of sails in the Thames and is sent word of the Wantsum back (?)
a young thegn of Kent who learned his trade of war under him, and will one day buy a holy book back from the heathen with gold (?)

lines.greet: A merchant, and from Frisia. Then you have seen their ships closer than I have. How many keels, and where? Count, do not guess.
lines.greet_again: You count well. I want you on the down at dawn with my watchman. You know a trader's sail from the other kind.
rumour: We took nine of their ships off Sandwich. Nine. The king has the best one. I asked for the second and got the fourth.
They mean to winter on the island. No army has done that here. If they do, somebody is feeding them, and I will know who.
Huda is bringing the men of Surrey. With his and mine we go over at the ebb. Stay off the strait that day.
lines.saying: A fleet is only men who cannot swim, standing on wood.
lines.warned: Do not sell them corn. I will not ask twice, and I will not ask at all if I find your sacks in their camp.
lines.farewell: Go. And if you see sails where there should be none, come back and tell my man at the toll. It will be remembered.

people.source: historical: Ealhhere, ealdorman of Kent, named 839 to 853; with King Æthelstan he fought in ships at Sandwich in 851 and took nine; killed on Thanet in 853 with Huda of Surrey, 'many men slain and drowned on either hand' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851, 853, Ingram 1823). That he came to Sarre is ours, from the fight on the island; his looks and words are ours. An ealdorman takes the role 'chief' (npc_roles_793.json)

people.name: Leofnoth
people.trait: The king's reeve at the crossing in the tribute years: the man who reckoned Sarre's part of East Kent's three thousand pounds, carried it to the fleet himself, and has kept the tally sticks.
people.want: The tallies believed: that every hide and every hull paid what he says it paid, and that none of it stuck to him.
people.fear: A second reckoning; a king who asks where the first one went.
people.voice: Tired, exact, courteous. Counts aloud under his breath, and says 'the army' for the Danes even after one of them is king.
people.looks: About forty in 1009, stooped, thin fair hair, a good grey cloak gone shabby, a rod of office, a bag of split tally sticks and a folding balance on his belt.
knows: what each landing in East Kent paid toward the three thousand pounds, and who is still behind
where the fleet lies and which of its captains can be bargained with
what the new pennies are worth against the old and when they must be changed
whose kin were carried off in 1011, and what is asked for them
after 1023, what is Christ Church's at Sandwich and what is still the king's here

ties.note: the moneyer at Gipeswic paid the same army in his own town; they write to compare losses
weighed East Kent's silver out before Thorkell's man in 1009, and was told to his face it was light
after 1016 the king's reeve still, under a king whose army he once paid to go away
sends a boy riding to the toll man at Lundenwic when a fleet lies in the strait: a day of warning for the river
a boy of Dofras who came out with the town's ships in the reeve's last summers and was counted with the men (?)

lines.greet: A Frisian keel. You trade here, so you are in the reckoning. It is by the hull. I did not make it, I only carry it.
lines.greet_again: Your stick is here, both halves. Paid in full, the autumn the fleet came. I wish every hide on the island could say it.
rumour: They came to Sandwich soon after Lammas. Three thousand pounds from East Kent alone. I weighed it out myself and was told it was light.
The archbishop would not let himself be bought. They killed him with ox bones at their feast. Their own captain tried to stop it, I am told.
The king has given the saint to Canterbury. The island stood in the road. I was sent to move it. I am not thanked on either side.
lines.saying: Peace is the dearest thing I ever bought, and I have had to buy it again every year since.
lines.tally: Keep your half of the stick. Kings change. The notches do not, and the next reeve will ask.
lines.farewell: Go by the north mouth. The south one is full of other people's ships. God keep you from being counted twice.

people.source: invented; no reeve of Sarre is named in any text (dossier 8). East Kent's three thousand pounds, 'soon after Lammas', are the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1009; Archbishop Ælfheah's death and Thorkell's offer for him are the Chronicle for 1012 and Thietmar (?) (spine, cast.thorkell); the moving of Saint Mildrith in 1030 against the island is the dossier (5). The tie to Gipeswic answers places/gipeswic.json (gipeswic.leofsige)

stories.title: Worn out with great age
stories.summary: While the two kings keep their shores shut, the minster has no wine for the altar, and its oldest ship is no longer fit to fetch any. The old king's charter lets the nuns put another ship in her place, and a Frisian hull under the abbess's cross is not a Frankish hull, if the toll man can be brought to see it.
stories.picture: The strand at slack water under a pale sky: an old patched ship on rollers before a shed with a cross over its doors, a small nun with a wax tablet standing between a lean toll man and a merchant, and a little Frisian boat afloat behind them with one cask in her.

beats.text: Cwenburh shows you the oldest ship and says the charter's words over her: broken, worn out with great age, or lost by wreck, which God forbid. The minster needs four casks of wine before Easter and none can land at Lundenwic. She asks what a Frisian would want for fetching it.
Cwenburh orders wine for the altar from whoever can bring it: four casks before Easter, at the minster's price, and more than the price in a year when no Frankish cask may land at Lundenwic.

Dunwalh will pass a cask that is the minster's when it lands. A cask that is yours until it is sold is Frankish goods in a shut year, and the wic-reeve Wighelm is on the strand today in his green cloak, asking the same question twice.

Abbot Gervold's clerk will let wine for an English altar leave, quietly, if it is written down as the abbess's and a letter goes with it to the reeve at Lundenwic. He seals the letter and does not say what is in it.

Wighelm reads the clerk's letter, asks who gave it to you, asks again, and lets the minster's wine and its carrier be. He says the nuns of Thanet have had a ship free on this strand since his grandfather's day.

The charter's last clause: what a replaced ship earns by her trading must be offered to the king at Fordwic. The king's man there takes the first season's gain, or takes a look and a gift, depending on who is king that month.
The letter of King Charles is read on the strand: the ports are open. Cwenburh names the master of the house's ship for the coming year before the toll man and two witnesses.

endings.how: Fetched the wine as the abbess's own, carried the clerk's letter to Lundenwic, and offered the first season's gain at Fordwic without being asked.
endings.text: Your boat is named before witnesses as the ship that stands in the old one's place. A cross is nailed to her stem. Dunwalh cuts no notch for her and says his counting has always been at fault.
endings.reward: The abbess's freedom at Sarre and Fordwic (unlock_charter_sarre): toll none on this ship; a standing commission for the minster's wine, wax and corn; Cwenburh a fast friend; the thread's flags bs_ban_heard and bs_letter are set and cleared on the way.

endings.how: Landed the wine as your own and sold it to the minster by night at twice the price.
endings.text: The Mass is said. Cwenburh pays to the penny and does not ask you to sit. Dunwalh, who saw the cask go up the bank, cuts a notch and keeps the stick.
endings.reward: Silver, about a good voyage's worth; no charter; the toll man is wary and searches this house's ships at Sarre until Offa is dead.

endings.how: Took the minster's ship but kept back her gains from the king's man at Fordwic.
endings.text: The clause is read out to you by a reeve who has it by heart. The ship goes back to the nuns and the season's profit goes to the king, with something over.
endings.reward: A fine and a hard lesson in charters; the minster's ship is closed to this house for the life of the king; Wighelm remembers your name, which is not a gift.

stories.reward: The abbess's freedom from toll and her trade, or a cask's profit and a watched hull, or a fine: each a different standing with the nun, the toll man and the reeve at Lundenwic.

stories.title: Heavier than their sins
stories.summary: Three English pilgrims wait at the crossing for a ship to the Franks' shore, on their way to Rome, and one of them carries a bundle the ferryman says is heavier than their sins. King Charles has complained of men who join the pilgrims to dodge the toll, and what a skipper does with these three is told on both shores.
stories.picture: The ferry stakes at low water in the evening: three men in travel-stained cloaks with staffs sitting on an upturned boat, one of them with his arm over a tight bundle, the ferryman pointing at it with his pole and laughing, a small merchant boat lying ready behind.

beats.text: Their letters of passage were written at Christ Church. Whether there were three letters or two was settled in the porch there, by what a skipper said to the scribe.

Three for the thresholds of the Apostles, come over from Canterbury, with no silver but their prayers and their hands at the oars. Dudda carried their bundle and winks. They ask a passage to the wic on the Canche.

Tidburh has fed them two days on trust. The quiet one eats like a man used to better and knows the price of a short cloak at Saint-Denis. She asks you, if you take them, to carry a word to her cousin Wulfgifu.

The toll men let true pilgrims through free, by the king's word. They open bundles when a skipper looks sideways. Twelve English cloaks are a pilgrim's baggage or a trader's stock, according to who is telling it.
The monk Osmund takes the two true ones into the guest hall and asks after a ferryman of Thanet he has never met. Wulfgifu, in the street behind, wants to hear about a blue cup.

Nine more wait on the shingle at Dofras, and the boatman there says two of them walk like men who have carried cloth all their lives. Dudda says the Dofras men drown their pilgrims; Wulfric says the Wantsum men bore theirs to death.

endings.how: Carried all three for nothing and asked no questions.
endings.text: Two go on to Rome and pray for you by name at every shrine on the road. The third sells his cloaks at the fair and is back at Sarre by Martinmas, greeting you like a brother in front of the toll man.
endings.reward: The deed of carrying pilgrims; the crew's hearts lifted; Tidburh and Osmund friendly; a false pilgrim who remembers you and brings a rumour worth silver once a year.

endings.how: Asked about the bundle, and took a share of the cloaks' sale for keeping quiet.
endings.text: The cloaks sell well in a year when no English cloth should be there at all. At the Canche the toll men look twice at your boat from then on, and the true pilgrims do not look at you.
endings.reward: Silver, a fair voyage's worth, and a partner for English cloth while the ports are shut; a risk at the Quentovic toll on each later call; the pious man's good word lost.

endings.how: Told the toll man at Sarre, or the one at Quentovic, what was in the bundle.
endings.text: The cloaks pay their toll and a little more. The two true pilgrims cross with you all the same, and the abbot's clerk writes your name down as a skipper who knows the king's law.
endings.reward: Standing with the toll at Sarre and at Quentovic; a letter of passage from the abbot's clerk, good until the peace of 796; one enemy with a long memory and a short cloak.

endings.text: They wait for the next boat. Tidburh's word to her cousin waits with them.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but a little of Tidburh's regard; the word can still be carried.

stories.reward: Prayers and a yearly rumour, or cloth silver and a watched hull, or the toll men's trust on two shores; and either way Tidburh hears from her cousin if you carry the word.

stories.title: Who weighs with an emperor
stories.summary: Bynna's plough turns up a small bronze balance on a chain and a set of weights made from old emperors' coins rubbed flat: a money man's tools, laid in the ground with him before anyone here was baptised. The priest says they go back, the toll man says they are the king's, and Bynna thinks a merchant is the only one who would use them.
stories.picture: A brown furrow under the green down in spring light: a bony ploughman holding up a tiny green balance by its chain, eight oxen standing, a merchant crouched to look at small round weights laid out on a flat stone, gulls behind.

beats.text: Bynna shows you the little pan and nineteen weights, some with a worn head still on them. He asks what such a thing weighs out. With these a man weighed gold and silver from over the sea, when Kent had kings of its own and no pennies.

Dunwalh has a balance of his own for clipped and foreign silver. He sets the old weights against Offa's new heavy penny and they agree with nothing. He says found metal is the king's; he says it without getting up.

The priest from Reculver says the scale was laid with a dead man and should lie with him, and a Mass said for whoever he was. He does not say it would be a sin to weigh with it. He says it would be like eating off a grave.

A moneyer who signs the king's coin looks at the weights a long time. Two of them match the gold pieces the Frisians still bring; one matches the Danes' ounce. He offers silver for the set, or an afternoon's teaching for a loan of it.

Eoba at Canterbury sets the old weights against his own, one by one. Two match the gold pieces the Frisians bring, one the Danes' ounce. For a loan of the set he teaches what each is for, and how a cut piece is tried with a knife.

endings.how: Bought the balance from Bynna, had the moneyer teach its weights, and carried it north.
endings.text: The old pan hangs in your sea chest. Beyond the Eider, where no stamp counts and silver is cut and weighed, the buyers see a man who brought his own scale and stop leaning on theirs.
endings.reward: A folding scale and the knowledge of the weights (the thread's flag sv_scale): northern buyers stop cheating this house; Bynna a friend who keeps the next find for you.

endings.how: Paid for a Mass at the cross and had the scale laid back in the down.
endings.text: The priest says the Mass for a man with no name. Bynna ploughs round the place afterwards. The island hears that the Frisian paid for a stranger's soul.
endings.reward: Standing with the church of Reculver and with the minster; the nun opens the house's trade a year sooner; Bynna thinks you soft and likes you for it.

endings.how: Handed it to the toll man as the king's.
endings.text: Dunwalh takes it with great solemnity and puts it in the case with his own. It is not heard of at any king's hall.
endings.reward: The toll man is your friend for life and passes you at the slack without a notch, now and then; Bynna shows you nothing more.

stories.reward: A scale and its weights for the northern markets, or the church's good word, or the toll man's: and each of the three men remembers which you chose.

stories.title: Whom do you mean to sell to
stories.summary: In the years when the heathen men first stay the winter on Thanet, the strait is a market with two buyers: an army on the island with silver and no bread, and an ealdorman at the toll post who wants ships counted and corn kept from the camp. A merchant can see more from the down than either of them.
stories.picture: Dawn on the bare down above the strait: a big man in a red cloak and mail beside a watchman and a merchant, all three shading their eyes at a line of dark sails off the far headland; below them the landing empty but for one small boat.

beats.text: The toll man does not ask what you carry. He asks whom you mean to sell to. Behind him stands the ealdorman Ealhhere, back from Sandwich with nine prizes, who asks how many keels you passed and where.
From the down you can tell a trader's sail from the other kind, and the watchman cannot. Ealhhere wants you up here at first light for as many days as you will give.

Ceolmund on the Strand sends word down the river of sails in the Thames and is sent word of the Wantsum back. After the storm of 851 he counts the ealdorman's nine prizes among the hulls he would run to.
Three hundred and fifty ships have come into the Thames mouth, and the city two miles up the track from Fordwic is stormed. The road from the gate to the landing is full of people who want a keel.

The watcher on the east height at Dofras counts what goes through the strait and sends a boy along the cliff. His count and the count from the down at Sarre are a tide apart, and the ealdorman wants both.
A man with a Danish way of speaking wades out to your boat at dusk. The camp will pay in cut silver, three times the strand's price, for corn and ale. He names a creek and a tide.
The men of Kent and the men of Surrey go over to the island at the ebb. For a while they have the better of it. By evening both ealdormen are dead, and the ferry carries back what the water gives up.

endings.how: Counted sails for the ealdorman and sold nothing to the camp.
endings.text: Your count goes to the king with Ealhhere's name on it. After the fight on the island his widow sends a gilded cup to the Frisian who stood on the down, and the toll at Sarre does not forget whose friend you were.
endings.reward: A gift of plate; standing with the West Saxon king's men in every Kentish port for a generation, inherited; a deed of warning carried.

endings.how: Sold corn to the camp by night.
endings.text: The silver is good and is cut honestly. Somebody saw the boat. Nothing is said at the toll post, and nothing is forgotten.
endings.reward: Silver, three good voyages' worth in one night; the Danes of that fleet know this house and let it pass at sea; the reeves of Kent are wary to shunned until the king who knows of it is dead.

endings.how: Sold to the camp and counted for the ealdorman.
endings.text: It works until the day the two accounts meet. Doubtful: either Ealhhere dies on the island before he hears, or he hears.
endings.reward: The silver and the gift together if the luck holds; if it does not, the boat is seized at Sarre and the house pays to get her back.

stories.reward: A king's men's friendship that outlives you, or the camp's silver and a closed shore, or both for as long as nobody compares notes.

stories.title: Landing and water
stories.summary: Thanet learns over two hundred years what a fleet off the Foreland costs: it promises money in 865 and is harried anyway, robs merchants and is plundered by its own king, is overrun in 980, and pays its part of three thousand pounds to Thorkell in 1009. In 1048 the islanders try the other thing, and deny twenty-five ships both landing and water. The house that has traded here through all of it is asked each time which side of the strand it stands on.
stories.picture: The strand under a hard bright sky: a line of island men with spears, bill-hooks and boat poles standing in the shallows, a row of long ships lying off with their oars out, and between them one small trading boat hauled up, her crew passing water casks up the bank and out of reach.

beats.text: The men of Kent have promised the army on the island money for peace, and the toll post is collecting toward it. The army takes the promise and goes inland by night all the same.

The strand is half burnt and very honest. The king had the whole island plundered because its people robbed merchants out of York. A York man in the ale-house tells it with relish; the island tells it differently.
The ship-army has been over Thanet. The cross is down and somebody has set it up again with rope. The priest asks for wax, and for word of who was carried off and where they are sold.

Thorkell's fleet lies at Sandwich and East Kent is buying peace for three thousand pounds. The reeve reckons the landing's part and asks each ship that trades here for hers. Thorkell's own man comes up the strait to see it weighed.
The moneyer at Gipeswic paid the same army in his own town, and writes to Leofnoth to compare losses. Neither letter is cheerful and both are exact.
A boy rides from the Wantsum to the tollman at Billingsgate whenever a fleet lies in the strait: a day of warning for the river, paid for in news of what London will give.

The saint has been carried off to Canterbury by the king's gift, and the island stood in the road to stop it and was moved aside. The shed with the cross over its door is Saint Augustine's now. An old woman spits when she says so.

Twenty-five ships have stripped Sandwich and are coming about the island. The land's folk are on the shore with whatever has an edge. They want every boat hauled up, every cask emptied or hidden, and a merchant who knows how raiders think.

Earl Godwine's ships come round from Dofras, where they took what ships and hostages they chose, and go through the strait past Sarre to the North-mouth and London. The island counts them and does not stand in the road.

endings.how: In 1048, hauled the boat up, gave the house's casks and stood on the strand with the island.
endings.text: The ships lie off a day, find neither a beach nor a spring that is not held against them, and go over the sea to sell what they took at Sandwich. Thanet does not forget who stood in the water.
endings.reward: The island's friendship, inherited: lodging and stores free at Sarre, the first sight of Thanet's corn each Lammas, and men for a crew whenever asked; the deed is told at Sandwich and in Lundenwic.

endings.how: Paid the house's part of each tribute when the reeve asked, and kept out of the rest.
endings.text: The tallies show this house paid in 865 and in 1009. It is treated as a neighbour in the reckoning and a stranger in the fight, which is fair.
endings.reward: The thread's flag en_paid_share; standing with the king's reeves; no toll at Sarre in any year the house paid toward a tribute.

endings.how: Traded with the fleets when they lay at Sandwich.
endings.text: A fleet buys corn, ale and news at a fleet's prices and sells what it has taken for less than it is worth. The profit is real. So is the look on the strand the next spring.
endings.reward: Silver, and cheap plundered goods to carry away; Thorkell's men know the house; Sarre and Fordwic are cool to wary for the life of the heir who did it.

stories.reward: A place on the island that your heirs keep, or the reeves' respect, or the fleets' custom: the island has a long memory and tells each new toll man which it was.

stories.title: The Sheldrake
stories.summary: Tidburh's husband took a ship called the Sheldrake out by the North-mouth nine summers ago with corn for the Strand, and no word has come back. On the breaking beach at Lundenwic a clinker ship is coming apart for her iron, and the wright who bought her can say where she was found. What a merchant tells the widow, and how, is his to choose.
stories.picture: A wright on a gravel beach holding up a short carved stem-piece shaped like a duck's head, half a stripped hull behind him, a Frisian master turning the carving over in his hands under a grey sky.

beats.text: Tidburh asks every master bound for the Thames the same thing: if you hear of a ship called the Sheldrake, tell me, whatever it is. She says it lightly and does not look up from the oysters.

A hull is coming apart plank by plank. The wright bought her from a Kentish man who found her on the sands in the river mouth nine summers back, mast gone, nobody aboard, corn sprouting in her bilge. Her stem-piece is a carved sheldrake's head. He will give it for the asking.
Wynflaed remembers that summer: a corn factor who waited a week on the hard for a Thanet ship, drank on the stick, and went home without paying. She has the notches still.
You are back at the crossing with a carved duck's head in your sea chest. Tidburh is opening oysters, and asks what wheat was at Lundenwic.

endings.how: Brought her the stem-piece and told her where the hull was found.
endings.text: She holds it a while and sets it on the shelf above the ale tub, facing the door. Dudda, who never stops talking, says nothing for the length of a crossing. The priest from Reculver says a Mass for four men.
endings.reward: Tidburh a fast friend: lodging and the first cup free at Sarre, and every price she hears told to you first; the flag ese_sheldrake_told.

endings.how: Told her the ship was sold sound in the north and her husband went with the buyer.
endings.text: She thanks you, and asks which port, and what he looked like now. She has kept an ale-house twenty years. She fills your cup herself and does not ask again.
endings.reward: Nothing gained: she is a little cooler than she was; the flag ese_sheldrake_lied. The truth can still be brought.

endings.how: Said nothing, and left the carving on the beach or in the chest.
endings.text: She goes on asking every master bound for the Thames. One day one of them will tell her, less gently, and add whose keel lay beside the wreck and said nothing.
endings.reward: Nothing lost. The stem-piece, if kept, is a thing in the chest that any Thanet man will know.

stories.reward: A widow's friendship on the strait where every price passes twice. The story costs a tide and some courage, and nothing else.

works.name: A hard of chalk and hurdles
works.what: A causeway of wattle hurdles pegged into the mud and packed with chalk rubble, from the bank down to the low-water channel, so that a boat can be loaded and unloaded at any state of the tide.
works.needs: The toll man at least friendly; chalk from the bank is free, the hurdles and the labour are not.
works.gives: No waiting for the tide to load at Sarre; porters cost half; the island calls it by your house's name while it lasts, and it wants mending every ten years.
works.picture: A pale straight path of chalk and woven hurdles running out over grey mud to a small boat, men with baskets on it, the white bank behind.
works.source: invented in the period's manner: brushwood and hurdle hards are known at other English tidal landings of these centuries (?); nothing is dug at Sarre

works.name: A new boat for the crossing
works.what: The wright builds the ferryman a broad new boat of Kentish oak to replace the one that has been patched on trust for two winters.
works.needs: The wright and the ferryman both at least easy with you.
works.gives: The crossing is free to this house and its people for as long as the boat lasts; the ferryman teaches the two fords and the channel to both mouths without being paid (toward unlock_pilot_wantsum); every traveller to Canterbury hears whose boat he is in.
works.picture: A broad new clinker boat, still yellow, being pushed down the stakes into the water by a short strong man and a wright with an axe.
works.source: invented; the price and the six weeks are those of a small working boat (unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_west_small_boat). A ferry here is likely, not recorded, before about 1414

works.name: A watch on the down
works.what: A hut for a watchman on the top of the down, a horn, a stack of furze kept dry for a fire, and a man's keep for the sailing season. From there both mouths of the strait and the sea off the Foreland can be seen.
works.needs: A year in which ships have been seen that did not come in; the leave of the king's reeve or the ealdorman.
works.gives: Warning at Sarre of any fleet in the strait or off the Foreland a tide before it comes: time to load and go, or to haul up and hide; the ealdorman's and the island's good word.
works.picture: A small turf hut and a stacked beacon on a bare green hilltop, a man with a horn looking out over a wide strait and the sea beyond.
works.source: invented. The down commands 'the country for miles around' (Brent 1863); Sheppey was harried in 835; Kentish charters of the 9th century speak of service against the heathen (?). No beacon at Sarre is recorded

works.name: A bay in the abbess's shed
works.what: One bay of the minster's ship-house, with a bar and the nun's eye on it, for goods waiting on the other tide.
works.needs: The nun at least easy with you; nothing stored that the minster would be ashamed of.
works.gives: Store up to a boatload at Sarre for a season; goods under the minster's roof are not counted at the toll post until they are sold.
works.picture: The inside of an oak shed: oars in a rack, bins of corn, and in one bay a few casks and bales behind a wooden bar with a tally stick hung on it.

works.name: A light for Saint Mildrith
works.what: Wax enough to keep a candle burning before the saint's body at Minster for a year, given in the house's name on her day.
works.needs: To be at Sarre in the days before her feast, thirteen days into July, with wax or the price of it.
works.gives: The house is prayed for by name at Minster; the abbess hears of it; the island's people, who walk to the feast, are friendlier at the market for a year.
works.picture: A dim wooden church crowded with country people, one tall candle burning before a shrine hung with cloth, a nun trimming the wick.
works.source: Saint Mildrith's body lay at Minster in the church Abbess Eadburh built before 748, until 1030 (Sawyer 91; dossier 2, 5, 6). The gift is ours; wax for church lights is everywhere a merchant's alms

ships.how: bought second-hand, or built to order in six weeks
ships.note: The boat of the strait: six metres, four oars, for nets, weirs, oysters and the ferry. The wright on the strand builds them between the minster's jobs, and a fisherman's widow usually has one to sell.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat with four oars drawn up on shingle under a white chalk bank, nets drying over her gunwale.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat; unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_west_small_boat names Sarre

ships.how: lent by the abbess to a trusted master, not owned; or built to order over a winter
ships.note: The ships of the charter: small coasters that work Thanet, the Wantsum and the Thames free of toll. The minster lends one to a merchant who has kept three of its commissions; two thirds of the freight on the house's own goods is the house's.
ships.picture: A broad double-ended coaster of ten or eleven metres afloat off the strand, one mast, a small wooden cross nailed to her stem, a nun on the bank counting jars into her.
ships.source: Sawyer 29, 86, 91; ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship; story/ships_793.json (built at Sarre; lent at the minsters until about 870); unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_coaster_minster_ship

ships.note: Frisian and Kentish boats of the house's own size pass every tide, and now and then a skipper who has had enough of the Foreland sells one on the strand.
ships.picture: A small open trading boat with her mast down, lying on her bilge in the mud, a man walking round her knocking on the planks.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json gislinge; that one is for sale here is ours

ships.how: hired by the crossing, with the ferryman
ships.note: The broad flat boat of the crossing. She can be hired for a day to lighten a ship that has taken the mud, or to carry stock over to the Kent shore.
ships.picture: A wide flat boat with two oars at the end of a line of stakes, a horse standing in her and a short man holding its head.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json ferry_barge; the crossing as in sarre.ferry (likely, not recorded before about 1414)

sayings.text: The flood comes in at both doors and meets itself at Sarre.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, from Hasted (1800): the tides flow in at both mouths and meet here

sayings.text: A man who weighs silver for strangers needs his spear as much as his scale.
sayings.source: invented, turning the 1866 editor's remark on the man buried at Sarre with a balance, weights, shield and spear: his weapons were 'no doubt, a very essential part of his stock-in-trade' (Archaeologia Cantiana 6)

sayings.text: About three furlongs over, and fordable only in two places.
sayings.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.25, of the Wantsum (L.C. Jane's translation, 1903)

sayings.text: Blow your horn or be taken for a thief.
sayings.source: the sense of the Law of Wihtred 28 (695), not its words: a stranger off the track who neither shouts nor blows his horn

sayings.text: No snakes on Thanet, and no secrets either.
sayings.source: the first half is Isidore of Seville, about 620, through the dossier (7); the second half is ours

sayings.text: They denied them as well landing as water.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1046 for 1048, of the people of Thanet (Ingram 1823, with Giles's additions)

sayings.text: The toll man asks whether a ship with every plank renewed is the same ship. The wright says: ask the keel.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the replacement clause of Sawyer 29 and the old puzzle of the mended ship

sayings.text: A Frank asked the nun why her ship was so old. She said: because the king's charter is older, and the two must agree.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: a proverb turned, on the replacement clause of Sawyer 29

sayings.text: Three ships free, says the charter. Four, says the toll man. The fourth is the Holy Ghost, says the nun, and pays no toll either.
sayings.source: invented, a clerk's joke of the kind a monk writes in a margin; the three ships are Sawyer 29

easter_eggs.text: At low water the ferryman carries his passenger out to the boat on his shoulders. A map-maker drew exactly this at Sarre six hundred years after the game begins.
easter_eggs.source: the Thanet map of about 1414 (Perkins 2007; Brent 1863)

easter_eggs.text: The yellow bone counters on the ale-house board came out of the down. Two graves there held ninety such counters between them, and two dice.
easter_eggs.source: Brent, Archaeologia Cantiana 6 (1866) and 7 (1868): graves 6 and 198

easter_eggs.text: Bynna's thunder stone is a fossil sea-urchin. A woman was buried on the down with one, beside six gold pendants, 133 amber beads and a crystal ball in a silver sling.
A bag of Thanet earth, sold by the ferryman, is said to kill snakes in any land it is carried to. A Frank or a Frisian who has read Isidore will pay for it, once.
easter_eggs.source: Isidore of Seville, Etymologies, about 620, through the dossier (7)

easter_eggs.text: The Britons' name for the island was Ruim. An old shepherd on the down still uses it for the far end, where he does not go.
easter_eggs.source: the name is in the dossier (7); the shepherd is ours

easter_eggs.text: From the down, on a clear day, a line of darker grass runs across the island by Minster. It is the track of the tame hind that ran round the land King Ecgberht gave for two murdered princes. The king's man Thunor, who killed them, was swallowed by the earth.
easter_eggs.source: the Kentish royal legend; Hasted (1800) for the hind's track as the boundary of Minster and Monkton (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: The minster's first ship was bought from a man called Leubucus: a Frankish name on an English charter. Cwenburh can still tell you what was paid, and that it was too much.
easter_eggs.source: Sawyer 91 (748); the price is not recorded and she does not name it

easter_eggs.text: Now and then a small thick silver piece without a king's name turns up in change. Dunwalh will not take them; fifty have been found at Reculver, more than anywhere in England but Hamwic.
At Ebbsfleet, by the south mouth, a rock is shown with a footprint in it where Saint Mildrith stepped ashore from Francia.
easter_eggs.source: the Kentish royal legend, through the dossier (7)

unlocks.what: The abbess's freedom from toll at Sarre and Fordwic, on your own hull
unlocks.how: End 'Worn out with great age' as the master the nun names; or master one of the minster's ships.
unlocks.gives: unlock_charter_sarre: toll none on this ship at Sarre and at Fordwic; it lapses if captives or arms are carried under it, if standing with the minster falls, and when the king who confirmed it dies, until an audience and a gift renew it.

unlocks.what: One of the minster's coasters for a season
unlocks.how: Keep three commissions for the minster and be well regarded at Sarre; then the nun asks.
unlocks.gives: unlock_ship_coaster_minster_ship: the class coaster_minster_ship, lent; two thirds of the freight on the house's own goods is the minster's.

unlocks.what: The Wantsum by heart: both fords, both mouths, and where the tides meet
unlocks.how: Hire Dudda as pilot on three calls and come through without touching; or pay for his new boat.
unlocks.gives: unlock_pilot_wantsum: learn (the Wantsum); no pilot is needed and nothing is doubtful in the strait for this house; inherited.

unlocks.what: The ploughman's riddle, on a leaf
unlocks.how: Trade Bynna a riddle he has not heard, on the headland of his strip.

unlocks.what: The oyster's riddle, and a bed for the night
unlocks.how: Eat Tidburh's oysters and guess what speaks without a mouth.
unlocks.gives: give_text exeter_77_oyster (unlocks_793.json text.exeter_77_oyster); the riddle's reward rw_lodging: lodging free at her house.

unlocks.how: Be a fast friend of the toll man, or end 'Who weighs with an emperor' by handing him the scale.
unlocks.gives: At Sarre, toll is sure to be asked only one call in two, while Dunwalh lives.

unlocks.what: A neighbour's place on Thanet, for the house and its heirs
unlocks.how: End 'Landing and water' on the strand with the island in 1048, or keep the watch on the down paid for twenty years.
unlocks.gives: lodge, store and provision free at Sarre; hire_crew never refused; the first sight of the island's corn each Lammas (buy_at_source).
